29988.e: The Diet, with its Catholic majority, invited people to Baden and set the rules. Baden was a common lordship and a usual meeting place of the Confederates.
29988.m: The Catholic cantons called the meeting in Baden in 1526.

29989.q: Whose successor did Heinrich Bullinger become in Zurich in 1531?
29989.e: After Zwingli's death at Kappel, Bullinger became minister at the Grossmünster at the end of 1531. He led the Zurich church for over 40 years.

29990.q: In which church did Heinrich Bullinger preach in Zurich?
29990.e: Like Zwingli before him, Bullinger was minister at the Grossmünster. From there he led the Zurich church for over 40 years.

29991.q: Heinrich Bullinger was born in Bremgarten in 1504. In which present-day canton is Bremgarten?
29991.e: Bremgarten is a small town on the river Reuss in the canton of Aargau. Bullinger's father was a priest there.
29991.m: Bullinger came from Bremgarten in Aargau.

29992.q: What is Heinrich Bullinger's “Second Helvetic Confession”?
a: A summary of the Reformed faith
A peace treaty with the Habsburgs
A law book of the city of Zurich
29992.e: In it Bullinger wrote down what Reformed Christians believe. It appeared in 1566 and was accepted by Reformed churches in many countries.
29992.m: The Second Helvetic Confession sums up the Reformed faith.

29993.q: With which Geneva reformer did Bullinger reach agreement on Holy Communion in 1549?
29993.e: In the Zurich Agreement (Consensus Tigurinus) of 1549, Bullinger and Calvin came to an agreement. This brought the churches of Zurich and Geneva closer together.
29993.m: Bullinger and Calvin reached agreement in 1549.

29994.q: What is Heinrich Bullinger especially famous for among historians?
29994.e: Around 12,000 of Bullinger's letters have survived. He was in contact with scholars and princes all over Europe.
29994.m: Bullinger wrote thousands of letters all over Europe.

29995.q: Why did Protestants from Locarno have to leave their home and move to Zurich in 1555?
a: Because they were not allowed to stay in Catholic Locarno
Because an earthquake destroyed the town
Because they found work as fishermen in Zurich
Because Locarno was sold to Italy
29995.e: The Catholic cantons that ruled Locarno would not tolerate the Protestants. Zurich took them in under Bullinger, and some of them set up silk businesses there.
29995.m: In 1555 Zurich took in Protestant refugees from Locarno.

29996.q: What job did Heinrich Bullinger have in Zurich for over 40 years?
a: He was mayor of the city
29996.e: As Antistes, Bullinger was the chief minister of the Zurich church. He held this office from 1531 until his death in 1575.
29996.m: Bullinger led the Zurich church for over 40 years.

29997.q: What were the French Protestants called?
29997.e: Calvin's followers in France were called Huguenots. Because they were persecuted, many fled to Reformed areas such as Geneva.
29997.m: The French Protestants were called Huguenots.

29998.q: What happened in Paris on St Bartholomew's Night in 1572?
a: A great fire destroyed the city
29998.e: On St Bartholomew's Night, 24 August 1572, thousands of Huguenots were killed in Paris. Afterwards many survivors fled to Geneva.
29998.m: After St Bartholomew's Night in 1572, many Huguenots fled to Geneva.

29999.q: What did the Edict of Nantes of 1598 allow the Huguenots in France to do?
29999.e: King Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598. It gave the Huguenots freedom of religion until Louis XIV cancelled it in 1685.
29999.m: From 1598 the Edict of Nantes protected the Huguenots.

30001.q: Which craft did Huguenot refugees especially promote in Geneva?
30001.e: Many Huguenots were skilled craftsmen and merchants. They helped Geneva become a centre of watchmaking.
30001.m: Huguenots helped to build up Geneva's watchmaking.

30003.q: Why was Geneva also called the “Protestant Rome”?
a: Because it was a centre of the Reformed faith
Because it lies on seven hills
30003.e: Geneva meant to many Reformed Christians what Rome meant to Catholics: the most important centre for many Reformed Christians. Ministers were trained here and sent to other countries.
30003.m: Geneva counted as the Protestant Rome.

30004.q: In which year did the Escalade of Geneva take place?
30004.e: On the night of 11 to 12 December 1602, Savoyard troops tried to capture Geneva. The attack failed.
30004.m: The Escalade of Geneva was in 1602.

30006.q: What does the French word “escalade” mean?
30006.e: The Savoyard soldiers wanted to climb the city walls secretly at night. That is where the name Escalade comes from.
30006.m: Escalade means climbing up the walls.

30007.q: What did the Savoyard soldiers use to get over the walls of Geneva in 1602?
30007.e: The attackers brought ladders painted black so they could climb the walls at night without being seen. Some got in, but they were driven back.
30007.m: The Savoyards climbed the walls with ladders.

30008.q: According to legend, which woman of Geneva poured hot soup on an attacker?
30008.e: Catherine Cheynel, known as Mère Royaume, is said to have thrown a pot of hot vegetable soup at a soldier. She became the heroine of the Escalade.
30008.m: Mère Royaume fought back with a soup pot.

30009.q: Which sweet treat is part of the Escalade festival today?
a: A chocolate pot with marzipan vegetables
30009.e: In memory of Mère Royaume, a chocolate pot is smashed. Inside are little vegetables made of marzipan.
30009.m: At the Escalade people smash a chocolate pot.

30010.q: Which public race takes place in Geneva's old town every year at the Escalade?
30010.e: The Course de l'Escalade runs through Geneva's old town. Many runners take part in fancy dress.
30010.m: The Course de l'Escalade race is part of the Escalade.

30011.q: In which month does Geneva celebrate the Escalade every year?
30011.e: The attack was on the night of 11 to 12 December 1602. That is why the Escalade is celebrated every December.
30011.m: The Escalade is celebrated in December.

30012.q: At what time of day did the Savoyard soldiers attack Geneva in 1602?
30012.e: The soldiers came in the dark so that nobody would notice them. Even so, the people of Geneva woke up in time and fought back.
30012.m: The Savoyards attacked Geneva at night.

30013.q: Which city did Johann Rudolf Wettstein come from?
30013.e: Wettstein was born in Basel in 1594 and later became mayor of the city. He is seen as an important diplomat of the Swiss Confederation.

30014.q: Which office did Wettstein hold in his home city from 1645?
30014.e: Wettstein became mayor of Basel in 1645. In this role he travelled to the peace negotiations in Westphalia.
30014.m: Wettstein was mayor of Basel from 1645.

30015.q: Which war ended in 1648 with the Peace of Westphalia?
30015.e: The Thirty Years' War devastated large parts of Central Europe from 1618 to 1648. The Swiss Confederation was largely spared.
30015.m: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648.

30016.q: What did Wettstein achieve for the Swiss Confederation in 1648?
a: Independence from the Holy Roman Empire
The founding of the federal state
30016.e: In the Peace of Westphalia the Confederation was freed from the Empire. This made it a legally independent state as well.
30016.m: Since 1648 the Confederation has been independent of the Empire.

30017.q: Johann Rudolf Wettstein was a diplomat. What does a diplomat do?
a: Negotiates with other states for their country
30017.e: From 1646 to 1648 Wettstein negotiated for the Confederates in Münster in Westphalia with the Emperor's envoys.
30017.m: As a diplomat, Wettstein negotiated for the Swiss Confederation.

30018.q: What changed for Basel merchants in 1648 because of independence from the Empire?
a: Imperial courts could no longer judge them
They no longer had to pay taxes
They were no longer allowed to travel to Germany
30018.e: Wettstein's mission began because of lawsuits against Basel merchants at the Imperial Chamber Court. Once free of the Empire, that court no longer had any say.
30018.m: After 1648 imperial courts had no power over the Confederates.

30019.q: Which river does the Wettstein Bridge in Basel cross?
30019.e: The Wettstein Bridge links Grossbasel with Kleinbasel. Wettsteinplatz also reminds people of the mayor.
30019.m: The Wettstein Bridge honours Johann Rudolf Wettstein.

30020.q: What was Basel's religion in the time of Johann Rudolf Wettstein?
30020.e: Basel had been Reformed since 1529. In 1646 Wettstein first travelled to Westphalia on behalf of the Reformed cantons.
30020.m: Basel was Reformed in Wettstein's time.

30021.q: In which year did the great Swiss Peasants' War take place?
30021.e: The Swiss Peasants' War broke out in 1653. It was the biggest uprising of country people in the Old Swiss Confederacy.
30021.m: The Swiss Peasants' War was in 1653.

30022.q: In which valley in Lucerne did the Peasants' War of 1653 begin?
30022.e: The peasants of the Entlebuch were the first to rise up against the city of Lucerne. The uprising then spread to Bern, Solothurn and Basel.
30022.m: The Peasants' War began in the Entlebuch.

30023.q: Which Bernese farmer was the most important leader in the Peasants' War of 1653?
30023.e: Niklaus Leuenberger from Rüderswil in the Emmental was elected leader of the peasants. He led the negotiations with the cities.
30023.m: Niklaus Leuenberger led the peasants in 1653.

30024.q: What made things much worse for the peasants before 1653?
30024.e: After the Thirty Years' War, prices for farm produce fell. On top of that, Bern and Lucerne devalued their Batzen coins, so the peasants' savings were worth less.
30024.m: Falling prices and devalued coins drove the peasants to rise up.

30025.q: What did the rebel peasants do in Huttwil in May 1653?
30025.e: In Huttwil, peasants from several areas swore to help one another. The authorities saw this as a dangerous conspiracy.
30025.m: The peasants formed an alliance in Huttwil.

30026.q: How did the Peasants' War of 1653 end?
a: The peasants took over the cities
30026.e: An army of the Diet beat the peasants in June 1653. After that the uprising collapsed.
30026.m: The peasants lost the Peasants' War of 1653.

30027.q: What happened to Niklaus Leuenberger after the Peasants' War?
30027.e: They captured Leuenberger and executed him in Bern in September 1653. The cities wanted to scare people off from further uprisings.

30028.q: In which cantons was the Peasants' War of 1653 especially strong?
30028.e: The uprising began in the Entlebuch in Lucerne and spread to Bern, Solothurn and Basel.
30028.m: The Peasants' War mainly affected Lucerne, Bern, Solothurn and Basel.

30029.q: What was the Peasants' War of 1653 mainly directed against?
a: The power of the ruling cities
30029.e: The peasants demanded lower dues and more rights against their city lords. But the authorities of Bern, Lucerne, Solothurn and Basel won.
30029.m: In 1653 the peasants fought against the rule of the cities.

30030.q: In which canton is Villmergen, which gave its name to the Villmergen Wars?
30030.e: Villmergen lies in the Freiamt near Wohlen. Decisive battles took place there in 1656 and 1712.
30030.m: Villmergen lies in the Freiamt in Aargau.

30031.q: Who won the First Villmergen War in 1656?
30031.e: In January 1656 troops from Lucerne defeated the army of Bern at Villmergen. The Catholics stayed the leading power.
30031.m: In 1656 the Catholics won at Villmergen.

30032.q: Who won the Second Villmergen War in 1712?
30032.e: In July 1712 the Reformed cantons, led by Bern, won. This shifted the balance in favour of the Reformed side.
30032.m: In 1712 Bern and Zurich won at Villmergen.

30033.q: Which faiths faced each other in the Villmergen Wars?
30033.e: Both Villmergen Wars were religious wars within the Swiss Confederation. They were about power and faith between Catholic and Reformed cantons.
30033.m: In the Villmergen Wars Catholics fought against Reformed Protestants.

30034.q: Which conflict over a valley in present-day St Gallen started the war of 1712?
30034.e: The people of the Toggenburg resisted their ruler, the Abbot of St Gallen. Bern and Zurich supported them, while the Catholic cantons supported the abbot.
30034.m: The Toggenburg dispute led to war in 1712.

30035.q: What changed in the Swiss Confederation after the Second Villmergen War of 1712?
a: The Reformed cantons became more powerful
30035.e: After their victory, Bern and Zurich had more influence. In the shared territories, Reformed and Catholic people were given equal rights.
30035.m: After 1712 the Reformed cantons were stronger.

30036.q: How many times did Catholics and Reformed Protestants fight each other at Villmergen?
30036.e: Big battles took place at Villmergen in 1656 and 1712. That is why we speak of the First and Second Villmergen Wars.
30036.m: There were two Villmergen Wars, in 1656 and 1712.

30037.q: Roughly how many years passed between the two Villmergen Wars?
30037.e: The First Villmergen War was in 1656, the Second in 1712. That is 56 years apart.
30037.m: About 50 years passed between the Villmergen Wars.

30038.q: What were the few noble families who ruled Bern in the Ancien Régime called?
30038.e: In Bern only certain families eligible for office could be elected to the council. They are called patricians.

30039.q: Which of these cities was a patrician city in the Ancien Régime?
30039.e: Besides Bern, Lucerne, Fribourg and Solothurn were also ruled by a few old families. That is why they are called patrician cities.

30040.q: What did it mean in old Bern if a family was “eligible to rule”?
a: The family could hold government offices
The family had to provide soldiers
The family was allowed to trade
The family did not have to pay taxes
30040.e: Only members of families eligible to rule could get into the Great and Small Council. That kept power in a few hands.
30040.m: Only families eligible to rule could govern in Bern.

30041.q: Which event ended the rule of the patricians in 1798?
30041.e: In 1798 French troops marched in and the Old Swiss Confederacy collapsed. The new Helvetic Republic abolished the privileges of the patricians.
30041.m: The rule of the patricians ended in 1798.

30042.q: Which Zurich spring festival is still celebrated by the guilds today?
30042.e: At Sechseläuten the guilds parade through Zurich in costume. At the end the Böögg, a snowman figure, is burnt.
30042.m: The Zurich guilds celebrate at Sechseläuten.

30043.q: In which cities did the guilds have great political power in the Ancien Régime?
30043.e: In the guild cities, the guilds elected representatives to the council. So merchants and master craftsmen there had a share in governing.
30043.m: In Zurich, Basel and Schaffhausen the guilds helped to govern.

30044.q: Which region did Major Davel want to free from Bern in 1723?
30044.e: Davel wanted to free Vaud from the rule of Bern. The Bernese governed the area with their own bailiffs.
30044.m: Major Davel wanted to free Vaud.

30045.q: What did Major Davel hope for when he marched to Lausanne with soldiers in 1723?
a: That the city would join him against Bern
That the King of France would reward him
That he would become mayor of Bern
That the city would give him a castle
30045.e: Davel presented his plan to the council of Lausanne. But the city authorities betrayed him to Bern.
30045.m: In 1723 Davel tried to free Vaud.

30046.q: To which city did Major Davel march with his soldiers?
30046.e: Davel turned up in Lausanne with his troops and presented his plan to the council. But the city authorities betrayed him to Bern.

30047.q: Bern ruled Vaud from 1536 to 1798. Roughly how long was that?
30047.e: Bern conquered Vaud from Savoy in 1536. Only in 1798 did Vaud break away from Bern.
30047.m: Vaud was under Bernese rule for over 250 years.

30048.q: What happened to Major Davel after his failed attempt?
30048.e: They arrested Davel, sentenced him and beheaded him at Vidy in Lausanne on 24 April 1723. He stayed calm and composed to the very end.

30049.q: How is Major Davel seen in the canton of Vaud today?
a: As a saint of the Church
30049.e: The people of Vaud see Davel as an early fighter for their freedom. There is a statue of him in front of the castle in Lausanne.
30049.m: Major Davel is a Vaud hero of freedom.

30050.q: When did Vaud finally become independent of Bern?
30050.e: In 1798, with French support, Vaud declared itself independent of Bern. In 1803 it became a canton of Switzerland in its own right.
30050.m: Vaud broke away from Bern in 1798.

30051.q: Where in Lausanne is there a statue of Major Davel?
a: In front of the seat of the Vaud government
In the Federal Palace in Bern
30051.e: The statue stands in front of the Château Saint-Maire in Lausanne, the seat of the Vaud government. The Bernese bailiffs used to rule from there.
30051.m: Davel's statue stands in front of the government seat in Lausanne.

30052.q: What is Anna Göldi often called?
a: The first woman doctor in Switzerland
The founder of the Red Cross
30052.e: Anna Göldi was sentenced to death in Glarus. She is seen as one of the last women in Europe to be executed for supposed witchcraft.
30052.m: Anna Göldi is known as the last witch in Europe.

30053.q: In which year was Anna Göldi executed?
30053.e: Anna Göldi was executed in Glarus in June 1782. By then, the time of the witch hunts had really already ended.

30054.q: In which canton was Anna Göldi sentenced?
30054.e: The court in the cantonal capital of Glarus sentenced Anna Göldi. Officially they called the crime not witchcraft but poisoning.
30054.m: Anna Göldi received her sentence in Glarus.

30055.e: Anna Göldi worked as a maidservant in the house of the doctor Johann Jakob Tschudi. After a quarrel she lost her job and later faced charges.

30056.q: According to the charges, what was Anna Göldi supposed to have done to a girl?
30056.e: People said Dr Tschudi's daughter had spat out pins. They accused Anna Göldi of bewitching the child.
30056.m: Anna Göldi faced charges over supposedly bewitched pins.

30057.q: When was Anna Göldi officially cleared by the canton of Glarus?
30057.e: In 2008 the cantonal parliament and government of Glarus declared the verdict a judicial murder. This officially cleared Anna Göldi's name.

30058.e: Anna Göldi was beheaded, not burnt. Officially the verdict named murder by poisoning, not for witchcraft.
30058.m: Anna Göldi died by the sword.

30059.q: What does the term “judicial murder” mean in the case of Anna Göldi?
a: An execution based on an unjust verdict
30059.e: A judicial murder is the execution of an innocent person after a wrong verdict. The verdict against Anna Göldi was already called this in the 18th century.
30059.m: A judicial murder is an execution after an unjust verdict.

30061.q: Which present-day cantons were once mostly common lordships?
30061.e: Thurgau and Ticino were ruled jointly by several cantons for a long time. In 1803 they became cantons in their own right.
30061.m: Thurgau and Ticino used to be common lordships.

30062.q: How long did a bailiff usually stay in office in a common lordship?
30062.e: The ruling cantons took turns sending a bailiff. He usually stayed for two years, then it was another canton's turn.
30062.m: A bailiff usually ruled for two years.

30063.q: The Valtellina used to be a subject territory of the Grisons. Which country does it belong to today?
30063.e: The Three Leagues lost the Valtellina in 1797. Today the valley belongs to Italy and borders the Grisons.
30063.m: The Valtellina belongs to Italy today.

30064.q: Which castle in the canton of Zurich was the seat of the Zurich bailiffs from 1424 to 1798?
30064.e: A total of 59 Zurich bailiffs lived at Kyburg. Today the castle is a museum visited by many school classes.
30064.m: Kyburg was the seat of the Zurich bailiffs for a long time.

30065.q: Which canton ruled Vaud with bailiffs until 1798?
30065.e: Bern had conquered Vaud in 1536 and had it run by bailiffs. Only in 1798 did Vaud become free.

a: An administrator of a subject territory
30066.e: A bailiff ran a subject territory on behalf of one or more cantons. He collected dues and judged cases.
30066.m: A bailiff ran a subject territory.

30067.q: Where did a bailiff usually live?
30067.e: The bailiff lived and worked in the castle of his district. One example is the bailiff's castle in Baden.
30067.m: The bailiff lived in a castle.

30068.q: To whom did a bailiff have to account for how he ran his territory?
30068.e: The Diet was the meeting of envoys from the Swiss cantons. There the bailiffs of the common lordships presented their accounts every year.
30068.m: The bailiffs presented their accounts to the Diet.

30069.q: Which subject territory of Bern declared its independence with French support in January 1798?
30069.e: Vaud was a subject territory of Bern and declared the “Lemanic Republic” on 24 January 1798. Shortly afterwards French troops moved in.
30069.m: In 1798 Vaud was the first to break away from Bern.

30070.q: What did many people in Vaud want to free themselves from in 1798?
30070.e: Vaud was a subject territory of Bern for a long time. In 1798 it broke away with the help of France and later became a canton in its own right.
30070.m: Vaud freed itself from Bern in 1798.

30071.q: Which event in France came before the French invasion of 1798?
30071.e: The French Revolution began in 1789. Afterwards French troops carried the new ideas of liberty and equality into other countries.
30071.m: After the French Revolution the French came to Switzerland in 1798.

30072.q: Which model was the 1798 constitution of the Helvetic Republic based on?
30072.e: The constitution was written in Paris following the French pattern. It turned Switzerland into a single centralised state.
30072.m: The Helvetic constitution followed the example of France.

30073.q: Apart from money, what else did the French take from the Bern bear pit to Paris in 1798?
30073.e: The French troops took the Bern bears to Paris as spoils of victory. There they went to the zoo of the Jardin des Plantes.
30073.m: In 1798 even the Bern bears were taken to Paris.

30074.q: Which new state was created in 1798 after the French invasion?
30074.e: After the French marched in, the Helvetic Republic came into being. It lasted until 1803.
30074.m: The Helvetic Republic was created in 1798.

30075.q: What did supporters of the revolution put up in village squares in 1798 as a sign of the new freedom?
30075.e: The liberty tree was a symbol of the French Revolution. It was decorated with ribbons and a cap of liberty.
30075.m: In 1798 the liberty tree stood for the new freedom.

30076.q: What was new in the Helvetic Republic compared with the Old Swiss Confederacy?
a: There were no more subject territories
Only nobles were allowed to vote
30076.e: In the Helvetic Republic all citizens were meant to be equal before the law. The subject territories were set free.
30076.m: The Helvetic Republic abolished the subject territories.

30077.q: What did the people of Nidwalden refuse in summer 1798, which led to the French attack?
a: The oath to the Helvetic constitution
30077.e: Nidwalden refused to accept the new Helvetic constitution and swear the oath of loyalty. Then French troops attacked.
30077.m: In 1798 Nidwalden refused the oath to the Helvetic constitution.

30078.e: Because Nidwalden rejected the Helvetic constitution, French troops attacked. Whole villages were destroyed.

30079.q: In which year did the Days of Terror in Nidwalden take place?
30079.e: The fighting took place from 7 to 9 September 1798. That was the year the French marched into Switzerland.
30079.m: The Days of Terror in Nidwalden were in 1798.

30080.q: What did the Days of Terror of 1798 mean for many children in Nidwalden?
a: They had to move to France
They got a year off school
30080.e: Many parents were killed in 1798. Afterwards Pestalozzi looked after many orphans in Stans.
30080.m: After 1798 there were many orphans in Nidwalden.

30081.q: Roughly how many people from Nidwalden died in the Days of Terror in 1798?
30081.e: About 400 people died, including over a hundred women and 26 children. Whole villages burnt down.
30081.m: About 400 people from Nidwalden died in September 1798.

30082.q: Which place on Lake Lucerne was completely destroyed by the French in 1798?
30082.e: Stansstad, Buochs and Ennetmoos were completely destroyed. About 600 homes burnt down in Nidwalden.

30083.q: What do people in Nidwalden still call the events of 1798 today?
30083.e: In Nidwalden people speak of the “Franzosenüberfall”, the French Raid. The term became well known through a book by Franz Joseph Gut in 1862.
30083.m: In Nidwalden the event is called the French Raid.

30084.q: Where did Pestalozzi open a home for war orphans after the fighting of 1798?
30084.e: The Helvetic government asked Pestalozzi to run an orphanage in Stans. There he cared for many children whose parents had died.
30084.m: Pestalozzi looked after war orphans in Stans.

30085.e: Mediation comes from the French word for helping two sides agree. Napoleon acted as a go-between for the quarrelling Swiss parties.
30085.m: Mediation means helping two sides agree.

30086.q: In which city did Napoleon hand over the Act of Mediation in February 1803?
30086.e: Swiss delegates held talks at the Helvetic Consulta in Paris. On 19 February 1803 Napoleon handed them the Act of Mediation.
30086.m: The Act of Mediation was handed over in Paris in 1803.

30087.q: Who had the greatest influence on Switzerland during the Mediation period?
30087.e: Napoleon had issued the Act of Mediation. Switzerland had to follow France until 1813.
30087.m: During the Mediation period Napoleon decided over Switzerland.

30088.q: Which state came before the Mediation period?
30088.e: The Helvetic Republic existed from 1798 to 1803. Because it was divided by quarrels, Napoleon brought in the Act of Mediation in 1803.
30088.m: The Helvetic Republic came before the Mediation period.

30089.q: What did Switzerland have to provide for Napoleon after the alliance of 1803?
30089.e: Switzerland had to provide France with thousands of soldiers for its wars. Many never came back.
30089.m: Switzerland had to provide soldiers for Napoleon.

30090.q: Where did Napoleon march with his army in 1812, including many Swiss soldiers?
30090.e: In 1812 Napoleon attacked Russia. During the retreat in the icy winter most of the soldiers died, including many Swiss.
30090.m: In 1812 many Swiss fought with Napoleon in Russia.

30091.q: What ended the Mediation period at the end of 1813?
30091.e: After Napoleon's defeat at Leipzig, allied troops marched through Switzerland in December 1813. The Mediation government then stepped down.
30091.m: The Mediation period ended with Napoleon's defeat in 1813.

30092.q: Which area belonged to Austria before 1803 and then became part of the canton of Aargau?
30092.e: The Fricktal was Habsburg and Austrian for a long time. In 1803 it became part of the new canton of Aargau.
30092.m: The Fricktal passed from Austria to Aargau in 1803.

30093.q: Which canton has surrounded the two Appenzells since 1803?
30093.e: The canton of St Gallen was newly founded in 1803. It lies all around Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
30093.m: St Gallen surrounds the two Appenzells.

30094.q: Which town is the capital of the canton of Ticino today?
30094.e: Bellinzona has been Ticino's permanent capital since 1878. Before that, the seat of government moved between three towns.
30094.m: Bellinzona is the capital of Ticino.

30095.e: Several Swiss cantons ran Thurgau jointly as a subject territory. In 1803 it became a canton with equal rights.
30095.m: Before 1798 Thurgau was a common lordship.

30096.q: Which words have been on the coat of arms of the canton of Vaud since 1803?
30096.e: The motto “Liberté et Patrie” means “Freedom and Fatherland”. It is a reminder of the liberation from Bern.
30096.m: The Vaud coat of arms says Liberté et Patrie.

30097.q: Which old alliances did the canton of the Grisons grow out of?
30097.e: The Grisons used to be an associate of the Confederation made up of the Grey League, the League of God's House and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions. In 1803 it became a canton.
30097.m: The Grisons grew out of the Three Leagues.

30098.q: Which town became the capital of the new canton of Thurgau in 1803?
30098.e: Frauenfeld was already the bailiff's seat at the time of the common lordship. Since 1803 it has been the capital of the canton of Thurgau.
30098.m: Frauenfeld is the capital of Thurgau.

30099.q: Which town in Aargau is famous for its hot springs?
30099.e: Hot springs have bubbled up in Baden since Roman times. The County of Baden became part of the new canton of Aargau in 1803.
30099.m: Baden is famous for its hot springs.

30100.q: What is 1816 called, the year when it hardly got warm in Switzerland?
30100.e: 1816 was unusually cold and wet in Europe. That is why people speak of the “Year Without a Summer”.
30100.m: 1816 is called the Year Without a Summer.

30101.q: In which country is the volcano Tambora, whose eruption in 1815 caused the Year Without a Summer?
30101.e: Tambora is on the island of Sumbawa in Indonesia. Its ash darkened the sky all over the world.

30102.q: What fell several times down to low altitudes in Switzerland in summer 1816?
30102.e: Almost every month it snowed down to about 800 metres. In July snow even fell on the lowlands.
30102.m: In summer 1816 it snowed several times in Switzerland.

30103.q: What did starving people in Switzerland eat out of desperation in 1816 and 1817?
30103.e: Because there was no grain, people cooked grass and ate leaves, snails and unripe fruit. Reports from mountain areas said children grazed on grass like sheep.
30103.m: In 1817 many people were so hungry that they even ate grass.

30104.q: Which part of Switzerland suffered particularly badly from hunger in 1816 and 1817?
30104.e: In eastern Switzerland many people lived from textile work at home and had to buy expensive food. The hardship was especially great there.
30104.m: Eastern Switzerland suffered most from the famine.

30105.q: Why was there a great famine in Switzerland in 1816 and 1817?
a: Cold and rain ruined the harvest
A war destroyed all the fields
30105.e: After Tambora erupted it was cold and wet. Grain and potatoes did not ripen. Even Tsar Alexander I of Russia sent help to eastern Switzerland.
30105.m: Bad weather led to hunger in 1816 and 1817.

30106.q: By roughly how much did grain prices rise in German-speaking Switzerland by June 1817?
a: To two or three times as much
30106.e: In June 1817 grain cost about two and a half to three times as much as in 1815. In remote places it was even more expensive.
30106.m: In 1817 grain cost several times the normal price.

30107.q: Which famous novel was begun during the rainy summer of 1816 on Lake Geneva?
30107.e: Mary Shelley got stuck in the Villa Diodati with Lord Byron and friends because of the bad weather. There she began writing “Frankenstein”.
30107.m: Frankenstein was begun on Lake Geneva in the Year Without a Summer.

30108.q: Who had the great powers been fighting against until 1815?
30108.e: Austria, Russia, Prussia and Great Britain defeated Napoleon. Afterwards they reorganised Europe at the Congress of Vienna.
30108.m: After the victory over Napoleon, Europe was reorganised in 1815.

30109.q: Which word describes the neutrality the great powers guaranteed Switzerland in 1815?
30109.e: The powers recognised Switzerland's “permanent neutrality”. It was meant to last for ever, not just for one war.
30109.m: In 1815 Switzerland was granted permanent neutrality.

30110.q: At which congress did the powers negotiate the future of Switzerland in 1814 and 1815?
30110.e: After Napoleon's fall the great powers reorganised Europe in Vienna. Switzerland's borders and neutrality were also decided there.
30110.m: Switzerland was discussed at the Congress of Vienna.

30111.q: Which five great powers decided on the reorganisation of Europe in 1815?
a: Austria, Russia, Prussia, Great Britain, France
Ottoman Empire, Spain, Bavaria, Saxony, Russia
30111.e: Austria, Russia, Prussia and Great Britain had defeated Napoleon. France was brought back in as the fifth power.
30111.m: Five great powers reorganised Europe in 1815.

30112.q: Which country does the Valtellina, which used to belong to the Grisons, belong to today?
30112.e: The Valtellina was a subject territory of the Grisons until 1797. In 1815 it went to Austria, and today it is in Italy.
30112.m: The Valtellina belongs to Italy today.

30113.q: Which Swiss city was the neutrality of neighbouring Savoy meant to protect in 1815?
30113.e: Geneva is almost completely surrounded by France. That is why the area south of it also came under the neutrality.
30113.m: The neutrality of northern Savoy was meant to protect Geneva.

30114.q: Many people see a battle of 1515 as the start of Swiss restraint in wars. Which one?
30114.e: After their heavy defeat at Marignano, the Confederates gave up their policy of conquest. But their neutrality was only recognised in 1815.
30114.m: After Marignano in 1515 the Confederates kept out of the great powers' wars.

30115.q: What does neutrality mean for Switzerland when other states are at war?
a: It sends troops to both sides
It gives up its own army
30115.e: A neutral state does not take part in other states' wars. But it may defend itself.
30115.m: A neutral state does not take sides in other countries' wars.

30116.q: Which country did the Valais belong to from 1810 to 1813?
30116.e: Napoleon wanted to control the road over the Simplon and made the Valais part of France in 1810. In 1815 the Valais joined the Swiss Confederation.
30116.m: Under Napoleon the Valais belonged to France.

30117.q: Who was also Prince of Neuchâtel when it became a Swiss canton in 1815?
30117.e: Neuchâtel was a principality of the Prussian king and a Swiss canton at the same time. Only in 1857 did Prussia finally give it up.
30117.m: In 1815 Neuchâtel also belonged to the King of Prussia.

30118.q: In which year did Neuchâtel become a republic through a revolution?
30118.e: On 1 March 1848 republicans in Neuchâtel declared the republic. Prussia only recognised this in 1857.

30119.q: Which canton was given municipalities from Savoy and France after 1815 so that its territory would be joined up?
30119.e: Before that, foreign territory surrounded Geneva. With municipalities such as Carouge and Versoix it got a link to the rest of Switzerland.
30119.m: In 1815/16 Geneva was given municipalities from Savoy and France.

30120.q: What is the capital of the canton of Valais?
30120.e: Sion, Sitten in German, is the capital of the Valais. It has been the seat of a bishop for a long time.
30120.m: The capital of the Valais is Sion.

30121.q: Which city was annexed by France in 1798 before becoming a Swiss canton in 1815?
30121.e: France annexed Geneva in 1798 and made it the capital of the Léman department. In 1815 it joined the Swiss Confederation.

30122.q: Which present-day canton was formed from areas that went to Bern in 1815?
30122.e: In 1815 Bern was given large parts of the former Prince-Bishopric of Basel. In 1979 this became the canton of Jura.
30122.m: The canton of Jura used to belong to Bern.

30123.q: Until when was the Federal Treaty of 1815 in force?
30123.e: The Federal Treaty held the cantons loosely together. In 1848 the first Federal Constitution replaced it.
30123.m: The Federal Treaty was in force from 1815 to 1848.

30124.q: What was the assembly of cantonal envoys under the Federal Treaty called?
30124.e: Envoys from the cantons met at the Diet. They acted on the instructions of their cantonal governments.
30124.m: Under the Federal Treaty the Diet met.

30125.q: How many votes did a full canton have at the Diet from 1815?
30125.e: Each canton had one vote, no matter how big it was. Divided cantons such as Appenzell had half a vote each.
30125.m: At the Diet each canton had one vote.

30126.q: What did a special article of the Federal Treaty of 1815 guarantee the Church?
a: The election of bishops by the people
30126.e: The monasteries article guaranteed that the monasteries would continue to exist. That is why closing the monasteries in Aargau in 1841 was so controversial.
30126.m: The Federal Treaty protected the monasteries.

30127.q: What was missing under the Federal Treaty that made trade within Switzerland difficult?
30127.e: Each canton had its own coins, measures and customs duties. Only the federal state created the Swiss franc, from 1850.
30127.m: There was no common currency under the Federal Treaty.

30128.q: What did the cantons organise together under the Federal Treaty of 1815?
30128.e: The cantons provided troops together for defence. Schools, post and coins remained matters for each individual canton.
30128.m: Under the Federal Treaty the cantons defended the country together.

30129.q: What is the period from 1814 to 1830 called, when old privileges returned under the Federal Treaty?
30129.e: Restoration means bringing back. The old families in the cities regained much of their former power.
30129.m: Restoration means bringing back the old order.

30130.q: What does the word “Regeneration” mean in Swiss history?
30130.e: Regeneration means renewal. From 1830 many cantons gave themselves liberal constitutions.

30131.q: What did the liberals demand during the Regeneration?
a: Power should come from the people
Only nobles should be allowed to vote
30131.e: The liberals wanted popular sovereignty, meaning power comes from the people. They also wanted equality before the law, separation of powers and freedom of the press.
30131.m: In the Regeneration, power was to come from the people.

30132.q: Which freedom did the liberals demand so that newspapers could write without censorship?
30132.e: During the Restoration, newspapers were closely watched. The new liberal constitutions guaranteed freedom of the press.
30132.m: The liberals won freedom of the press.

30133.q: From which year did many cantons give themselves liberal constitutions during the Regeneration?
30133.e: After a revolution in Paris in 1830, many people in Switzerland also demanded more rights. Many cantons got new constitutions.

30134.q: What happened at the “Uster Fire” in 1832?
a: Home weavers set fire to a weaving mill
The army burnt down a village
30134.e: Home weavers feared that machines would take their work. So in November 1832 they set fire to the weaving mill in Uster.
30134.m: In the Uster Fire, home weavers destroyed a factory.

30135.q: What did the country people demand at the Uster Day in 1830?
a: More rights and a new constitution
30135.e: About 10,000 men from the countryside met in Uster in 1830. They demanded the same rights as the city citizens, and Zurich soon got a liberal constitution.
30135.m: At the Uster Day the country people demanded more rights.

30136.q: Who was against the liberals' reforms during the Regeneration?
30136.e: Conservative cantons such as Uri and Schwyz wanted to keep the old order. In 1832 they joined together in the League of Sarnen.

30137.q: Which college for teachers did the canton of Zurich found in Küsnacht in 1832?
30137.e: The liberals wanted good state schools for everyone. That needed well-trained teachers from the college in Küsnacht.
30137.m: Teachers were trained in Küsnacht from 1832.

30138.q: Which town became the capital of the new canton of Basel-Landschaft?
30138.e: Liestal has been the capital of Basel-Landschaft since the split. The cantonal parliament meets there.
30138.m: Liestal is the capital of Basel-Landschaft.

30139.q: Why did the countryside around Basel feel disadvantaged before 1830?
a: The city had more seats in parliament
The countryside had to speak French
The countryside was not allowed to build churches
30139.e: The city had about 40 per cent of the population but 60 per cent of the seats in the Great Council. The countryside demanded equal rights.
30139.m: The Basel countryside was under-represented in parliament.

30140.q: Into which two cantons was Basel divided in 1833?
30140.e: After fighting between city and countryside, the Diet split the canton in 1833. Since then there have been Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft.
30140.m: Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft have existed since 1833.

30141.q: Who won the decisive fight between the city and the countryside of Basel in 1833?
30141.e: In a battle near Frenkendorf, the city's troops were beaten. After that the canton was split completely.
30141.m: In 1833 the Basel countryside beat the city.

30142.q: Which municipality outside the city of Basel still belongs to the canton of Basel-Stadt today?
30142.e: Riehen and Bettingen, on the right bank of the Rhine, stayed with the city in 1833. Liestal, Muttenz and Allschwil belong to Basel-Landschaft.
30142.m: Riehen belongs to the canton of Basel-Stadt.

30143.q: What happened to the Basel Minster treasure after the split of the canton?
a: It was divided between the two parts
It stayed entirely in the city
30143.e: They divided the canton's property according to population, including the Minster treasure. The countryside later sold its share.
30143.m: In 1833 even the Basel Minster treasure got divided.

30144.q: What was the result of the 2014 vote on looking into a merger of the two Basels?
30144.e: Basel-Stadt voted yes with about 55 per cent, Basel-Landschaft voted no with about 68 per cent. That is why the two cantons remain separate.
30144.m: In 2014 Basel-Landschaft said no to the merger.

30145.q: In which year did the Züriputsch take place?
30145.e: On 6 September 1839 armed country people marched into the city of Zurich. The liberal government was overthrown.

30146.q: Who marched into the city of Zurich armed during the Züriputsch of 1839?
a: Country people from the surrounding area
30146.e: About 2,000 armed people from the countryside marched to Zurich. They were unhappy with the liberal government.
30146.m: In the Züriputsch, country people marched on Zurich.

30147.q: What happened to the liberal government in the Züriputsch?
30147.e: After the shooting on the Münsterplatz, the liberal government resigned. The conservatives took power.
30147.m: The Züriputsch overthrew the liberal government.

30148.q: What was the dispute before the Züriputsch mainly about?
30148.e: The government had appointed a controversial professor of religion. Many devout country people were outraged.
30148.m: The Züriputsch was about religion and the Church.

a: The violent overthrow of a government
30149.e: In a putsch, a government is removed by force or threats. That is what happened in Zurich in 1839.
30149.m: A putsch is the violent overthrow of a government.

30150.q: Roughly how many rebels died in the Züriputsch?
30150.e: In the clash on the Münsterplatz, 14 rebels died. Government member Hegetschweiler was also killed.

30151.q: How long did the conservatives rule in Zurich after the Züriputsch?
30151.e: The conservative government only lasted from 1839 to 1845. After that the liberals ruled again.
30151.m: After the Züriputsch the conservatives ruled only briefly.

30152.q: Which cantonal government were the Freischaren raids aimed at?
30152.e: The Freischaren wanted to overthrow the conservative government of Lucerne. They also wanted to drive the Jesuits out of Lucerne.
30152.m: The Freischaren raids were aimed at Lucerne.

a: Armed volunteers without orders from a government
30153.e: The Freischaren were groups of volunteers who armed themselves. In 1844 and 1845 they marched against Lucerne on their own initiative.

30154.q: How did the Freischaren raids against Lucerne end?
30154.e: Both Freischaren raids failed. In the second raid in 1845 many volunteers were killed or captured.
30154.m: The Freischaren raids against Lucerne failed.

30155.q: Which religious order did the Freischaren want to drive out of Lucerne?
30155.e: Lucerne had brought the Jesuits into its schools. Many liberals saw this as a danger and marched against Lucerne because of it.
30155.m: The Freischaren wanted to drive the Jesuits out of Lucerne.

30156.q: Which war did the dispute, made worse by the Freischaren raids, lead to in 1847?
30156.e: The Catholic conservative cantons founded the Sonderbund. In 1847 the Sonderbund War broke out, and the liberal cantons won it.
30156.m: After the Freischaren raids came the Sonderbund War of 1847.

30157.q: Which famous Zurich writer took part in the second Freischaren raid?
30157.e: Gottfried Keller went along as a young man in 1845 but did not fight. He was a committed liberal.
30157.m: Gottfried Keller took part in the second Freischaren raid.

30158.q: Which political side did the Freischaren volunteers belong to?
30158.e: The volunteers were liberals and radicals. They wanted to overthrow the Catholic conservative government in Lucerne.

30159.q: What did the Freischaren raids lead the Catholic conservative cantons to do?
30159.e: The conservative cantons felt threatened and joined together in their own alliance. This made the conflict worse, up to the war of 1847.
30159.m: The Freischaren raids sharpened the dispute between liberals and conservatives.

30160.q: In which city did Guillaume-Henri Dufour grow up and later work as an engineer?
30160.e: Dufour was born in Konstanz in 1787 but grew up in Geneva. Later, as an engineer, he built bridges and quays there.

30161.q: In which country was Dufour trained as an engineer and officer?
30161.e: Dufour studied at the École polytechnique in Paris from 1807 to 1809. After that he became an officer in the French army.

30162.q: In whose army did the young Dufour serve as an officer?
30162.e: From 1810 to 1814 Dufour was one of Napoleon's officers on the island of Corfu, where he built fortifications.
30162.m: As a young officer Dufour served under Napoleon.

30163.q: What kind of bridges did Dufour build as an engineer in Geneva?
30163.e: From 1823 Dufour built three suspension bridges made of wire cables in Geneva. The Passerelle de Saint-Antoine is seen as the world's first permanent wire cable suspension bridge.
30163.m: Dufour built wire cable suspension bridges in Geneva.

30164.q: Dufour taught at the military school in Thun. Which pupil later became Emperor of the French?
30164.e: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte attended the military school in Thun. He later became Emperor of the French as Napoleon III.
30164.m: Dufour taught the future Napoleon III.

30165.q: Which emblem for the federal troops goes back to Dufour?
a: A white cross on a red background
A red star on a white background
A golden lion on a blue background
A black eagle on a yellow background
30165.e: Dufour pushed for a single emblem for all the troops. The white cross on red became the Swiss flag.
30165.m: Dufour promoted the white cross on a red background.

30166.q: Dufour was elected general several times. When does Switzerland have a general at all?
a: Only in war or when war threatens
30166.e: Switzerland has no general in peacetime. The Federal Assembly only elects one when war threatens. Dufour was elected in 1847, 1849, 1856 and 1859.
30166.m: Switzerland only elects a general in times of war.

30167.q: Apart from his time as general, what is Dufour especially famous for?
a: The first accurate map of Switzerland
30167.e: Under Dufour the whole of Switzerland was surveyed. This produced the Dufour Map. Switzerland's highest peak, the Dufourspitze, is named after him.
30167.m: Dufour led the first national survey of Switzerland.

30168.q: In which year did the people accept the fully revised Federal Constitution?
30168.e: After a failed first attempt, the people and the cantons accepted the new Federal Constitution in April 1874. It came into force at the end of May 1874.
30168.m: The fully revised Federal Constitution dates from 1874.

30169.q: What happened to the first draft of a full revision of the Federal Constitution in 1872?
a: It never went to the vote
It was stopped by a court
30169.e: The 1872 draft wanted to make the federal government very strong and narrowly failed to win the people and the cantons. A watered-down draft passed two years later.
30169.m: The first revision draft of 1872 narrowly failed.

30170.q: Which area was much more centralised under federal control by the 1874 Federal Constitution?
30170.e: Training and arming the army was now largely the job of the federal government. Before that, the cantons had equipped their troops in very different ways.
30170.m: With the 1874 constitution the federal government took the lead in military matters.

30171.q: Which freedom did the 1874 Federal Constitution newly guarantee in full for the whole of Switzerland?
30171.e: Anyone who wanted to run a business or trade could now in principle do so anywhere in Switzerland. Cantonal barriers were removed.
30171.m: Since 1874 the constitution has protected freedom of trade and business.

30172.q: Which form of marriage became compulsory throughout Switzerland in 1874, the year of the new Federal Constitution?
30172.e: The constitution placed marriage under the protection of the federal government. A federal law of 1874 required marriage before a civil registrar, and a church wedding then became optional.
30172.m: Since 1874 people in Switzerland have married at the civil registry office.

30173.q: What happens if enough signatures are collected for an optional referendum?
a: The people vote on the law
30173.e: If the referendum succeeds, the people decide at the ballot box. Only if they say yes does the law come into force.
30173.m: After a referendum the people decide on the law.

30174.q: How many signatures does an optional referendum at federal level need today (as of 2025)?
30174.e: Since 1977, 50,000 valid signatures have been needed, collected within 100 days.
30174.m: Today a referendum needs 50,000 signatures in 100 days.

30175.q: What can you challenge with an optional referendum?
a: The election of a Federal Councillor
30175.e: The optional referendum is used against decisions of parliament, especially federal laws. If it succeeds, the people decide at the ballot box.
30175.m: With a referendum the people can have a vote on a new law.

30176.q: What majority is needed in a vote after an optional referendum?
a: Only a majority of the people
A majority of the people and of the cantons
Only a majority of the cantons
30176.e: In an optional referendum only the majority of voters decides. Unlike with changes to the constitution, a majority of the cantons is not needed.
30176.m: In an optional referendum only the majority of the people counts.

30177.q: Which kind of referendum has existed at federal level since 1848?
30177.e: From 1848 every change to the Federal Constitution automatically had to go to the people and the cantons. A referendum against laws was only added later.
30177.m: The people have had a mandatory vote on constitutional changes since 1848.

30178.q: How many signatures did a popular initiative need when it was introduced in 1891?
30178.e: At first 50,000 signatures were enough. Because the population grew and women gained the vote in 1971, the number was doubled in 1977.
30178.m: In 1891 a popular initiative needed the signatures of 50,000 voters.

30179.q: What majority does a popular initiative need to be accepted?
a: A majority of the people and of the cantons
Only a majority of the people
Only a majority of the cantons
A majority of the Federal Council
30179.e: A popular initiative changes the constitution. That is why both the majority of voters and the majority of cantons must agree.
30179.m: An initiative needs a yes from the people and the cantons.

30180.q: What did the first federal popular initiative to be accepted (1893) demand?
a: A ban on slaughter without stunning
The introduction of women's right to vote
30180.e: The initiative demanded that animals must be stunned before slaughter. In 1893 it became the first popular initiative to be accepted.
30180.m: The first successful popular initiative in 1893 was about slaughter without stunning.

30181.q: What can you demand with a federal popular initiative?
a: A change to the Federal Constitution
A change to a court judgement
The removal of a Federal Councillor
A new cantonal border without a vote
30181.e: With a popular initiative, citizens propose an addition or change to the Federal Constitution. The people and the cantons then vote on it.
30181.m: With a popular initiative the people can change the Federal Constitution.

30182.q: How long does an initiative committee have to collect the signatures today (as of 2025)?
30182.e: From publication in the Federal Gazette there is a deadline of 18 months. If enough valid signatures are collected by then, the initiative has succeeded.
30182.m: For a popular initiative you have 18 months to collect signatures.

30183.q: Which means of transport did Alfred Escher promote above all?
30183.e: Escher founded and ran railway companies, for example the Swiss Northeastern Railway. He wanted to connect Switzerland with railways.
30183.m: Alfred Escher was a great promoter of the railway.

30184.q: Which company for a major Alpine railway project did Alfred Escher chair from 1871?
30184.e: Escher campaigned for a railway line through the Gotthard. Because the costs ran over budget, he had to step down as chairman in 1878.
30184.m: Alfred Escher was the first chairman of the Gotthard Railway Company.

30185.q: Where in Zurich is there a large monument to Alfred Escher?
a: In front of the main station
30185.e: The Escher monument has stood on Bahnhofplatz in front of Zurich main station since 1889. That fits, because Escher promoted the railway.
30185.m: Alfred Escher's monument stands in front of Zurich main station.

30186.q: Roughly how long was the line of the Spanish Brötli Railway?
30186.e: The line from Zurich to Baden was about 23 kilometres long. The train took about three quarters of an hour.
30186.m: The Spanish Brötli Railway ran on a line about 23 kilometres long.

30188.q: What powered the locomotives of the Spanish Brötli Railway?
30188.e: The first locomotives had a boiler in which water was heated by fire into steam. The steam drove the wheels.
30188.m: The first Swiss railway ran with steam locomotives.

30189.q: Since when have the Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) existed?
30189.e: The SBB started operating on 1 January 1902. Bit by bit they took over the big private railways.
30189.m: The SBB has existed since 1 January 1902.

30190.q: How did the people vote in 1898 on the federal government buying back the big private railways?
30190.e: Under the slogan “The Swiss railways for the Swiss people”, the people clearly accepted the buyback law. This cleared the way for a state railway.
30190.m: With the yes vote of 1898 the big railways were nationalised.

30191.q: Where are the headquarters of the Swiss Federal Railways?
30191.e: The SBB's head office is in the federal city of Bern. The railway still belongs to the federal government today.
30191.m: The SBB has its headquarters in Bern.

30192.q: Which famous railway line through the Alps belongs to the SBB today?
30192.e: The Gotthard Railway used to be a private railway and joined the SBB in 1909. The other railways belong to their own companies.
30192.m: The Gotthard Railway has belonged to the SBB since 1909.

30193.q: Why were the SBB lines electrified after the First World War?
a: Because of a shortage of coal
Because of too much water in tunnels
Because steam was banned in cities
Because of a treaty with Italy
30193.e: Switzerland had to import the coal for steam locomotives, and during the war it ran short. Electricity from hydropower made the country more independent.
30193.m: Because of the coal shortage, the SBB soon ran on electricity from hydropower.

30195.q: Which battle did Henry Dunant witness in 1859 and then write about?
30195.e: In northern Italy Dunant saw thousands of wounded soldiers with no help. With women from the area he organised emergency care.
30195.m: Henry Dunant witnessed the Battle of Solferino in 1859.

30196.q: What is the name of the book in which Henry Dunant described his experiences on the battlefield?
a: The Cross on a White Background
30196.e: The book came out in 1862 and suggested an aid organisation for wounded soldiers. People read it all over Europe.
30196.m: Dunant's book “A Memory of Solferino” led to the founding of the Red Cross.

30197.q: In which year was the committee founded in Geneva that became the International Committee of the Red Cross?
30197.e: Five citizens, including Henry Dunant, founded the committee in 1863. Today it is called the International Committee of the Red Cross.
30197.m: The Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863.

30198.q: Which Swiss general belonged to the founding committee of the Red Cross?
30198.e: General Dufour, known from the Sonderbund War, became the first president of the committee. He brought the group a lot of respect.
30198.m: General Dufour helped to found the Red Cross.

30199.q: Where does the Red Cross emblem come from?
a: It is the Swiss flag with the colours swapped
It is the coat of arms of Geneva
It is an old church symbol from Rome
It is the badge of the doctors of Solferino
30199.e: In honour of Switzerland, they chose a red cross on a white background. They simply reversed the colours of the Swiss flag.
30199.m: The Red Cross is the Swiss flag reversed.

30200.q: Which treaty to protect wounded soldiers was signed in 1864?
30200.e: Twelve states signed the agreement in Geneva in 1864. Medics and the wounded were to be protected in war.
30200.m: The first Geneva Convention of 1864 protects wounded soldiers.

30201.q: During which war did the Bourbaki Army come to Switzerland in 1871?
30201.e: In the war against Prussia and its allies, the French Army of the East had been pushed back into the Jura. Its only way out led into Switzerland.
30201.m: The Bourbaki Army fled to Switzerland in the Franco-Prussian War.

30202.q: Roughly how many French soldiers of the Bourbaki Army were interned in Switzerland in 1871?
30202.e: About 87,000 men crossed the border at the start of February 1871. For little Switzerland this meant a huge task.
30202.m: About 87,000 Bourbaki soldiers found refuge in Switzerland in 1871.

30203.q: What did the French soldiers of the Bourbaki Army have to hand over when they crossed into Switzerland?
30203.e: The Treaty of Les Verrières of 1 February 1871 laid down that the French would be disarmed.
30203.m: The Bourbaki soldiers had to hand over their weapons at the border.

30204.q: Why did Switzerland only take in the Bourbaki Army without weapons in 1871?
a: Because weapons were banned in Switzerland
Because the soldiers wanted to sell them
30204.e: A neutral country must not let foreign troops carry on fighting. So General Hans Herzog demanded complete disarmament.
30204.m: As a neutral country, Switzerland only took in the Bourbaki Army disarmed.

30205.q: How were the interned Bourbaki soldiers housed in Switzerland?
a: All in one camp in Bern
Only in the canton of Neuchâtel
30205.e: The Federal Council spread the soldiers across all cantons except Ticino. Many municipalities helped with shelter and food.
30205.m: The Bourbaki soldiers were housed in almost every part of Switzerland.

30206.q: Where can you see a huge circular painting of the Bourbaki internment today?
30206.e: The Bourbaki Panorama by the painter Edouard Castres shows the army crossing the border. The round painting is over 100 metres long.
30206.m: The Bourbaki Panorama is in Lucerne.

30207.q: Who paid the costs of the Bourbaki internment in the end?
30207.e: France paid Switzerland back the costs of over 12 million francs. In March 1871 the soldiers went home.
30207.m: France paid Switzerland back the costs of the Bourbaki internment.

30208.q: What did the federal Factory Act of 1877 regulate?
30208.e: The law limited working hours, banned child labour in factories and protected workers in accidents.
30208.m: The Factory Act of 1877 protected factory workers.

30209.q: Under the Factory Act of 1877, what was the maximum length of a normal working day?
30209.e: The law introduced the eleven-hour day. Before that, many people in factories worked 13 hours or more a day.
30209.m: The Factory Act of 1877 limited work to 11 hours a day.

30210.q: From what age were children allowed to work in factories under the Factory Act of 1877?
30210.e: Children under 14 were no longer allowed to work in factories. This was also meant to let them go to school.
30210.m: From 1877 factory work was banned for children under 14.

30211.q: Who checked whether factories kept to the Factory Act of 1877?
30211.e: The federal government appointed factory inspectors who visited businesses and reported abuses. One of the first was the doctor Fridolin Schuler.
30211.m: Factory inspectors made sure the Factory Act was followed.

30212.q: In which industry did especially many people work in Swiss factories in the 19th century?
30212.e: Thousands of men, women and children worked in spinning and weaving mills. Cantons such as Glarus and Zurich had many textile factories.
30212.m: In the 19th century many people worked in textile factories.

30213.q: Which work did the Factory Act of 1877 ban for women?
30213.e: Women were no longer allowed to work in factories at night and on Sundays. For men there were many exceptions to these bans.
30213.m: From 1877 women in factories were protected from night and Sunday work.

30214.q: Under the Factory Act of 1877, what was the factory owner liable for?
30214.e: The factory owner had to be liable for physical injuries at work. This rule was extended in a separate liability law in 1881.
30214.m: Since 1877 factory owners have been liable for accidents at work.

30215.q: Where did many farming families in the Jura use to work on watch parts in winter?
a: At home in their living room
30215.e: In winter there was little to do on the farm. So many families made small watch parts at home, which were then put together.
30215.m: Many watch parts used to be made by people working at home.

30216.q: What forced Swiss watchmakers to build watch factories at the end of the 19th century?
a: A ban on working at home
30216.e: American factories made watches cheaply with machines. So the Swiss also began producing in factories.
30216.m: Competition from America led to watch factories in Switzerland.

30217.q: Who brought a lot of watchmaking knowledge to Geneva in the 16th century?
30217.e: Protestant refugees from France, the Huguenots, brought their craft skills with them. Because Calvin strictly limited jewellery, goldsmiths turned to watchmaking.
30217.m: Huguenots made Geneva an early watchmaking city.

30218.q: When did embroidery in eastern Switzerland reach its peak?
30218.e: Around 1910 embroidery was Switzerland's most important export. With the First World War and new fashions, sales collapsed.
30218.m: Embroidery boomed most just before the First World War.

30219.q: Around 1910 embroidery was Switzerland's most important export. Roughly what share of exports did it make up?
30219.e: At that time embroidery made up about 16 to 18 per cent of Swiss exports. That beat every other product.
30219.m: Around 1910 embroidery made up roughly one sixth of Swiss exports.

30220.q: Where was a large part of eastern Swiss embroidery made?
30220.e: Many families in Appenzell, Thurgau and the Toggenburg did embroidery at home on their own machines. They took the goods to the traders in St Gallen.
30220.m: Embroidery often meant work at home in the villages of eastern Switzerland.

30221.q: Which textile made St Gallen famous back in the Middle Ages and early modern times?
30221.e: St Gallen linen was sold to many countries in Europe. Later came cotton and finally embroidery.
30221.m: Before embroidery, St Gallen was known for its linen.

30222.q: Which country did most Swiss emigrants go to in the 19th century?
30222.e: The United States attracted people with cheap land and work. By far the most emigrants from Switzerland went there.
30222.m: Most Swiss emigrants went to the USA.

30223.q: What was an important reason for emigration from Switzerland in the 19th century?
a: An order from the government to leave
30223.e: Failed harvests, unemployment and poverty forced many people to seek their fortune elsewhere. Mountain regions were especially affected.
30223.m: Many people left Switzerland in the 19th century because of poverty.

30224.q: Which town in Brazil was founded in 1819 by emigrants from the canton of Fribourg?
30224.e: About 2,000 people, mostly from the canton of Fribourg, travelled to Brazil. Their settlement got the name of their home.
30224.m: Nova Friburgo in Brazil goes back to emigrants from Fribourg.

30225.q: Which settlement in Wisconsin (USA) did emigrants from a Swiss canton found in 1845?
30225.e: Poor families from the canton of Glarus founded the settlement. The town still keeps many Swiss customs today.
30225.m: New Glarus in the USA was founded by people from Glarus.

30226.q: Which event of 1816 caused a great famine and a wave of emigration?
a: The opening of the Gotthard Tunnel
30226.e: After a volcanic eruption in Indonesia, 1816 brought very cold and wet weather to Europe. The harvest failed, and many people in eastern Switzerland went hungry.
30226.m: The Year Without a Summer in 1816 brought hunger and emigration.

30227.q: Why did some municipalities pay for poor people's journey to America in the 19th century?
a: To save on the cost of poor relief
Because America paid them for it
30227.e: The municipalities had to look after their poor. A one-off crossing often cost them less than years of support.
30227.m: Some municipalities sent poor people to America to save money.

30228.q: What are the Swiss who live abroad today called?
30228.e: Besides the four language regions, the Swiss abroad form a symbolic Fifth Switzerland. They number over 800,000 people (as of 2024).
30228.m: The Swiss abroad are called the “Fifth Switzerland”.

30229.q: How many men fell to their deaths on the way down after the first ascent of the Matterhorn?
30229.e: Of the seven men, four fell when the rope broke. Only three survived.
30229.m: Four men died on the first ascent of the Matterhorn.

30230.q: From which country did a second roped party try to climb the Matterhorn first in 1865?
30230.e: The Matterhorn lies on the border between Switzerland and Italy. An Italian party reached the summit only a few days after Whymper.
30230.m: The Matterhorn lies on the border with Italy.

30231.q: What did the Federal Constitution of 1874 ban in connection with the Kulturkampf?
30231.e: In the conflict between the state and the Catholic Church, setting up new monasteries and orders was forbidden. This ban lasted until 1973.
30231.m: The 1874 constitution banned founding new monasteries.

30232.q: What does the word “optional” mean in the optional referendum?
a: Not compulsory, there is not always a vote
There must always be a vote
30232.e: Optional means not compulsory. A vote only takes place if enough signatures are collected.

30233.q: What happens if the people say no after an optional referendum?
a: The law does not come into force
A new Federal Council is elected
30233.e: If the majority of the people say no, the law is stopped. Parliament then has to look for a new solution.
30233.m: A no from the people stops the law.

30234.q: What can parliament put up against a popular initiative as its own solution?
30234.e: If the Federal Council and parliament partly like the idea, they can draw up a counter-proposal. The initiative is then often withdrawn.
30234.m: Parliament can set a counter-proposal against an initiative.

30236.q: In which century did Alfred Escher live and work?
30236.e: Alfred Escher lived from 1819 to 1882. He shaped the time when railways and banks were being created in Switzerland.
30236.m: Alfred Escher lived in the 19th century.

30237.q: What happened to Alfred Escher in 1880 when the Gotthard Tunnel broke through?
a: He set off the last blast
30237.e: After resigning as chairman of the Gotthard Railway, Escher had fallen out of favour. Nobody invited him to the breakthrough celebration in 1880, and illness kept him away from the opening in 1882.
30237.m: Alfred Escher got no invitation to the Gotthard Tunnel breakthrough.

30239.q: What nickname did opponents give Alfred Escher because of his great power?
30239.e: Escher held politics, banks and railways in one hand. Critics therefore spoke of the “Escher system” and called him “King Alfred”.
30239.m: Because of his power, opponents called Alfred Escher “King Alfred”.

30240.q: According to official figures, how many workers died building the Gotthard Tunnel?
30240.e: Officially 199 workers died in accidents. Many more fell ill or died later as a result of the hard work.
30240.m: About 200 workers died building the Gotthard Tunnel.

30241.q: What powered the drilling machines in the Gotthard Tunnel?
30241.e: At the tunnel entrances, water-driven machines compressed air. The compressed air drove the drills and brought some fresh air into the tunnel.
30241.m: The drills in the Gotthard Tunnel ran on compressed air.

30242.q: Which two neighbouring countries helped Switzerland pay for building the Gotthard Railway?
30242.e: Both countries wanted a fast rail link through the Alps. They supported the construction with large contributions.
30242.m: Italy and Germany helped to pay for the Gotthard Railway.

30243.q: What happened to the building contractor Louis Favre before the Gotthard Tunnel was finished?
a: He died in the tunnel in 1879
He went on to build the Eiffel Tower
30243.e: Louis Favre had a heart attack during an inspection in the tunnel in 1879. He did not live to see the breakthrough in 1880.
30243.m: Louis Favre died in the Gotthard Tunnel before it was finished.

30244.q: Which illness did many workers in the Gotthard Tunnel suffer from?
30244.e: Hookworm spread in the warm, damp and dirty tunnels. It made many workers anaemic and weak.
30244.m: Many Gotthard workers caught a worm disease.

30245.q: Who does the monument “The Victims of Labour” near Airolo station honour?
a: The workers who died building the tunnel
The mountain guides of the Matterhorn
The soldiers of the First World War
30245.e: The relief by Vincenzo Vela shows workers carrying an injured comrade out of the tunnel. It remembers those who died building the Gotthard.
30245.m: “The Victims of Labour” remembers the Gotthard workers who died.

30246.q: In which museum is there a replica of the first Swiss locomotive, the “Limmat”, today?
a: The Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne
The Watch Museum in La Chaux-de-Fonds
30246.e: The Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne shows trains, cars, ships and aircraft. It has a working replica of the “Limmat”.
30246.m: A replica of the “Limmat” locomotive is in the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne.

30247.q: In which year did a replica of the Spanish Brötli Railway run for the 100th anniversary of the Swiss railways?
30247.e: For the anniversary the whole train, locomotive included, was rebuilt. It still runs on special occasions today.
30247.m: A replica of the Spanish Brötli Railway was built for the 100th anniversary in 1947.

30248.q: In which canton was the terminus of the Spanish Brötli Railway?
30248.e: The railway ran through the Limmat Valley across the cantonal border. Its destination was the little spa town in the canton of Aargau.
30248.m: The Spanish Brötli Railway ended in the canton of Aargau.

30249.q: Who owned the big railways in Switzerland before the SBB was founded?
30249.e: Before 1902, private companies such as the Swiss Northeastern Railway or the Gotthard Railway ran the main lines. The federal government bought them back.
30249.m: The SBB grew out of several private railways.

30250.q: Which Alpine tunnel into the Valais opened in 1906 and was run by the SBB?
30250.e: The Simplon Tunnel links Brig with Domodossola in Italy. At the time it was the longest railway tunnel in the world.

30251.q: On which day is World Red Cross Day celebrated in honour of Henry Dunant's birthday?
30251.e: Henry Dunant was born on 8 May 1828. On this day Red Cross and Red Crescent societies all over the world remember their work.
30251.m: World Red Cross Day on 8 May is Dunant's birthday.

30252.q: Roughly how many horses did the Bourbaki Army bring with it into Switzerland?
30252.e: Besides the soldiers, about 12,000 horses had to be looked after too. Many were sick and completely starving.
30252.m: The Bourbaki Army brought about 12,000 horses with it.

30253.q: Which women workers did the Factory Act of 1877 especially protect?
30253.e: New mothers were not allowed to work in the factory for the first six weeks after the birth. This was meant to protect mother and child.
30253.m: The Factory Act protected pregnant women and young mothers.

30254.q: After which event was La Chaux-de-Fonds rebuilt in a chessboard pattern?
30254.e: In 1794 a fire destroyed large parts of the town. When people rebuilt it, they laid out straight, wide streets.
30254.m: After the fire of 1794, La Chaux-de-Fonds got a new chessboard layout.

30255.q: Why do many old watchmakers' houses in the Jura have so many large windows?
a: For plenty of daylight for the fine work
So that people outside can see the watches
30255.e: Watchmakers needed good light for the tiny watch parts. So their workbenches stood right by long rows of windows.
30255.m: Watchmakers needed lots of light, so they built houses with many windows.

30256.q: In which region of Switzerland are many well-known watchmaking towns?
30256.e: Towns such as La Chaux-de-Fonds, Le Locle and Saint-Imier lie in the Jura. Watches have been made there for centuries.
30256.m: The Jura is the home of Swiss watches.

30257.q: What powers a mechanical watch that has no battery?
30257.e: When you wind it up, you tighten a spring. The spring slowly releases its energy and so moves the hands.
30257.m: Mechanical watches run on a wound-up spring.

30258.q: Which machine stood in many living rooms in eastern Switzerland in the 19th century?
30258.e: Many families did embroidery at home on their own embroidery machines. That way they could stitch many patterns at the same time.
30258.m: In eastern Switzerland there was often an embroidery machine in the living room.

30259.q: What did the collapse of embroidery mean for eastern Switzerland after the First World War?
30259.e: Tens of thousands lost their jobs, and many embroidery machines were scrapped. Many people moved away.
30259.m: The decline of embroidery brought high unemployment to eastern Switzerland.

30260.q: What are the fine, openwork embroideries from eastern Switzerland called that look like lace and became world-famous?
30260.e: Special techniques created airy patterns that looked like real lace. They are still used in fashion today.
30260.m: St Gallen lace is a world-famous embroidery.

30261.q: Around what time did Switzerland change from a country of emigration to a country of immigration?
30261.e: With industry and railway building there was enough work by the end of the 19th century. Since then more people have come to Switzerland than have left.
30261.m: At the end of the 19th century Switzerland became a country of immigration.

30262.q: Where can you see the broken rope from the first ascent of the Matterhorn today?
a: In the Matterhorn Museum in Zermatt
In the National Museum in Zurich
In the Alpine Museum in London
On the summit of the Matterhorn
30262.e: The broken rope is one of the best-known exhibits in the museum at the foot of the mountain. It is a reminder of the accident of 1865.
30262.m: The broken rope from the Matterhorn is in the museum in Zermatt.

30263.q: In which village in the Valais at the foot of the Matterhorn did the first ascent begin?
30263.e: The roped party set off from Zermatt in 1865. Today Zermatt is a well-known holiday resort.
30263.m: The first ascent of the Matterhorn began in Zermatt.

30264.q: Which country did Edward Whymper, the leader of the first ascent of the Matterhorn, come from?
30264.e: Edward Whymper was English. In the 19th century many English climbers came to the Swiss Alps.

30265.q: What effect did the first ascent of the Matterhorn have on Zermatt?
a: The village became world-famous and attracted visitors
The village was declared a town
30265.e: The story of the first ascent went round the world. After that more and more tourists and climbers came to Zermatt.
30265.m: The first ascent made Zermatt world-famous.

30266.q: Which political force mainly pushed through the full revision of the Federal Constitution in 1874?
30266.e: The Radicals, supported by the Democrats, wanted a stronger federal government. The Catholic conservative cantons were mostly against it.
30266.m: The Radicals were the driving force behind the 1874 constitution.

30267.q: In which year did the border guard duty of the First World War begin?
30267.e: At the start of August 1914 the Federal Council ordered general mobilisation. For years afterwards the soldiers guarded the country's borders.
30267.m: Border guard duty began in 1914 with mobilisation.

30268.q: Which “trench” divided Switzerland during the First World War?
30268.e: Many German-speaking Swiss sided with Germany, many French-speaking Swiss with France. This divide was called the “trench”.
30268.m: In the First World War a trench divided German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.

30269.q: Why did many soldiers' families fall into hardship during border guard duty from 1914 to 1918?
a: There was no compensation for lost wages
30269.e: Anyone doing military service got no pay from their employer and no compensation for lost wages. Many families became poor because the breadwinner was away for months.
30269.m: Without compensation for lost wages, many soldiers' families suffered hardship in the First World War.

30271.q: What did Switzerland, as a neutral country, have to avoid in the First World War?
a: Favouring one side in the war
30271.e: Being neutral means keeping out of the war and not supporting either side. In 1917 a Federal Councillor had to resign because he had broken this rule.
30271.m: Neutral means not favouring one side in a war.

30272.q: Which big strike followed the hardship of the war years in November 1918?
30272.e: Many working families suffered hunger and hardship during the war. In November 1918 about 250,000 people went on strike all over Switzerland.
30272.m: The National Strike took place in November 1918.

30273.q: About which woman from the Jura did the soldiers on border duty sing a well-known song?
30273.e: Gilberte Montavon served the soldiers in the inn at Courgenay. The song about her became very popular, and a film about her came out in 1941.
30273.m: Gilberte de Courgenay became famous through a soldiers' song.

30274.q: In which year did the Swiss National Strike take place?
30274.e: The National Strike lasted from 12 to 14 November 1918. It is the biggest strike in Swiss history.
30274.m: The National Strike took place in November 1918.

30276.q: What did the strikers do during the National Strike of 1918?
30276.e: In a strike, people stop working to push through their demands. In 1918 the machines stood still in many factories.
30276.m: During the National Strike people stopped working.

30277.q: Roughly how many people took part in the National Strike of 1918?
30277.e: About 250,000 workers downed tools. Railway workers went on strike too, so in many places no trains ran.
30277.m: About a quarter of a million people took part in the National Strike.
